analysis.investment_thesis: A P/E of 2.64 is statistically enticing, but GB Logistics was only incorporated in 2019 and lacks the 5-10 year earnings record I demand. Without balance sheet data (current ratio, debt/equity, book value) and with a tiny INR 29.5 Cr market cap, this is speculation, not investment.
key_strengths: P/E of 2.64 is extraordinarily low — earnings yield ~38%
ROCE 28.2% and ROE 26.4% indicate strong capital efficiency
Promoter holding of 52.40% shows skin in the game
key_risks: Founded 2019 — no 5-year earnings record; likely a recent SME IPO
Market cap only INR 29.5 Cr — illiquid, manipulable, no institutional coverage (FII 0.29%)
No disclosed data on debt, current ratio, book value, or dividends
red_flags: Insufficient earnings history (<5 years) fails the Graham durability test
Trading of products alongside freight — low-moat commoditized business
Suspiciously low P/E often signals undisclosed quality or accounting concerns in micro-caps
No dividend history to verify real cash generation
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The numbers at first glance tempt the value hunter: a P/E of 2.64 implies an earnings yield near 38%, and returns on capital of 28% suggest the business earns real money on its assets. Were this a seasoned enterprise with a decade of audited statements, it would merit immediate investigation. But GB Logistics was incorporated in 2019 — barely seven years of existence, of which only a fraction is likely as a listed entity. My rule is unambiguous: at least five, preferably ten, consecutive years of positive earnings before a stock qualifies as an investment rather than a speculation.

Further, the data provided is dangerously incomplete for my framework. I have no book value (cannot compute the Graham Number or P/B), no current ratio (cannot verify liquidity >2.0), no debt-to-equity (cannot confirm balance sheet conservatism), and no dividend record. A INR 29.5 Cr market cap with negligible institutional ownership (FII 0.29%, DII 2.18%) is precisely the kind of micro-cap where Mr. Market's quoted price may have little relation to realizable value — and where a low P/E often masks earnings quality issues, related-party trading, or one-off items in a thinly-traded "trading of products" segment. Pass.
